title: Like his father
hookLine: Marcus on his adoptive father Antoninus: steady, unhurried, finishing what he began (Meditations 1.16)

cards: Some people make a room calmer just by walking into it. They don't talk much. They don't rush.
When they say they'll do something, it gets done, and nobody hears about it. You might have had a grandparent like that, or a coach, or a nurse on a night shift. Marcus Aurelius had one.

Not his birth father, who died when he was small, but the man who adopted him and raised him to rule: the emperor Antoninus. When Marcus reaches him, the list of debts suddenly turns into the longest entry in book one.

teach.b: Antoninus ruled Rome from 138 to 161. He adopted Marcus as a teenager, as part of the plan for who would come next, and Marcus lived beside him for years, watching. What he saw, he wrote down in Meditations 1.16.
It opens, in George Long's translation: "In my father I observed mildness of temper, and unchangeable resolution in the things which he had determined after due deliberation."
Mild, and immovable. Gentle, but once he'd thought it through, he finished it. The portrait runs a long page.
He wasn't vain about honors. He listened to anyone with something useful to say. He looked into things carefully in council and didn't settle for first impressions.
He was content with little, and cheerful. He took care of his body without fussing over it.
He never did anything in a rush, or so it looked, yet everything got done, in order, without strain. Later in the notebook, Marcus tells himself to do everything as a student of Antoninus would.
And an ancient biography that isn't always reliable tells how, on the day he died, Antoninus gave the palace guard their watchword for the night, and the word was equanimity.
Whether or not it happened, it fits the man Marcus remembered. Steadiness isn't slowness. It's doing one thing all the way, without panic, and then the next.

how: Some readers of the Meditations return to Marcus's portrait of Antoninus (1.16) as a picture of steady character, and some modern Stoics choose a real person they admire and ask what that person would do.

games.q: you're Antoninus, dying. the palace guard comes to ask for the night's watchword. what do you give them?
games.why: in the story, his last watchword was equanimity, aequanimitas. the source isn't always reliable, but it fits the steady man Marcus remembered.

practice: Pick something small that's waiting, a dish, a drawer, an email, a bed to make, and do just that one thing all the way to the end, at the speed of someone who has plenty of time, even if you don't.
When your mind jumps ahead, come back to your hands. When it's done, notice it's done, and let yourself feel it.

wordCard.voice: Antoninus, the emperor who adopted Marcus and raised him, remembered in Meditations as mild yet immovable. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: equanimity, an even mind. the watchword Antoninus is said to have given on his last day.

carryVoice: Your line: unhurried, finished. Marcus learned it by watching, for years. That's day one hundred sixty-nine.
